newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economy seen recovering from 1998 - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy seen recovering from 1998 - analyst.

text.p: Thailand's current economic slowdown is expected to persist for the next two quarters but the economy should show signs of recovery by 1998, an analyst at Fitch Investors Service LP said.

Peter Jordan, Fitch's international group managing director, told reporters that the Thai financial sector, weakened by over-exposure to the troubled property sector, would likely see the level of non-performing loans rise in the next few months before the position improved.
But Jordan said he was confident the Thai government could contain economic damage from what he termed cyclical problems faced by the property and financial sectors.
"I have no doubt in the government's ability to handle the problems and have not seen signs that its capability and resources would be overwhelmed by them," he said.
The analyst estimated that about 10 percent of outstanding loans extended by Thai commercial banks were non-performing.
The Thai authorities are encouraging more than 90 Thai finance and securities firms to consolidate through mergers and acquisitions to help them weather current problems.
Jordan described the Thai economic downturn as natural after the country experienced almost 10 years of unsustainable high growth in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

"What is unique (about Thailand) is that five to six percent growth is seen by some as a recession," he said referring to forecasts by private analysts that Thai gross domestic product growth would slow to about five percent in 1997 from 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent the previous year.
He said most economists expected Thai economic growth to stabilise at seven to eight percent a year after its current consolidation.

Fitch this week signed a three-year strategic partnership agreement with Thai Rating and Information Services (TRIS). The two agencies said the decision would help expand their expertise in rating new debt instruments.

Jordan said Fitch, a New York-based company founded in 1913, expected to complete its first sovereign rating on Thailand in the next few weeks but the Thai government has not indicated whether it would agree to release Fitch's rating.
He said Fitch released its ratings only on the consent of rated countries or companies and only did solicited ratings.
Jordan said Fitch was opening an office in Hong Kong to cover Asia where it has rated, or is in the process of rating, about five countries.
